title: The trie
sub: A node is a prefix: next[26] and an end flag, O(word length) per operation, a child dictionary and nodes in an array
cards/0/title: The problem and the signals of a trie
cards/0/body:
Implement Trie (LeetCode #208). Implement a prefix tree (trie) with three methods: Insert(word); Search(word) — is exactly this word stored; StartsWith(prefix) — does any stored word begin with prefix. Words are lowercase a–z, up to 2000 long, up to 3·10⁴ calls.

Signals of a trie:

1. The question is about a prefix: “starts with”, autocomplete, suggestions while typing.
2. One dictionary and many queries against it.
3. Words are built letter by letter, and after each letter you want to know whether any word continues that way — for example, while walking a grid of letters.

If you only need whole words, a HashSet<string> is enough. A trie is for when the question is about the beginning of a word.
cards/1/body:
HashSet<string>. Search is O(L) on average: the string's hash is computed over all its characters, then compared. But StartsWith scans all words: w.StartsWith(prefix, StringComparison.Ordinal) for each, O(n · L) per query. The hash of a prefix has nothing to do with the words — it cannot find the words that start with it.

All prefixes in a HashSet. On insert, add every prefix of the word: “a”, “ap”, “app”… A query is O(L), but a word of length L gives L prefixes with about L²/2 characters in total: for L = 2000 that is 2·10⁶ characters for one word, and every prefix is a new string on the heap.

A sorted array + binary search. Words sharing a prefix are adjacent in it: the first one ≥ prefix is found in O(L · log n). Good for a dictionary that never changes, but an insertion is O(n), a shift.

What repeats: words with a common beginning store and compare that beginning each on their own.
cards/2/q: A dictionary of 10⁴ words in a HashSet<string>, 3·10⁴ StartsWith queries by scanning. How many string comparisons in the worst case, and what follows?
cards/2/options/0: 3·10⁸ — that is seconds, a different approach is needed
cards/2/options/1: 3·10⁴ — one per query: the HashSet finds the prefix by its hash
cards/2/options/2: 10⁴ — each word is compared once across all queries
cards/2/explain: Every query with no match goes through all 10⁴ words: 3·10⁴ · 10⁴ = 3·10⁸ comparisons, each up to the prefix length in characters. At the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second, that is seconds.
cards/2/wrong/1: The hash of “app” has nothing to do with the hash of “apple”: a HashSet only answers questions about whole strings.
cards/2/wrong/2: The scan repeats on every query — words do not “remember” that they were compared already.
cards/3/body:
Glue the common beginnings together. A trie node is a prefix: the root is the empty string, an edge labelled c means “append c”. A node holds an array next[26], one slot per letter (next[ch - 'a']), and a flag end: “a stored word ends here”.

Insert walks from the root letter by letter; if an edge is missing, it creates the node. The last node gets end = true. Search and StartsWith walk the same way and answer false at the first missing edge. Reached the end: StartsWith is true right away, Search only if end is set. The flag is needed because the path “app” exists inside “apple” even if “app” was never inserted.

Words with a common prefix share its nodes: there are at most as many nodes as the total length of the words (plus the root), and usually far fewer. Every operation is O(L), where L is the word length, however many words the tree holds. Memory is O(nodes · 26).
cards/3/flow/2: no edge: Insert creates, lookups → false
cards/3/flow/3: end of the word: end = true
cards/3/flow/4: Search: path and end; StartsWith: path
cards/4/q: “tea”, “ten”, “to” and “inn” are inserted into an empty trie. How many nodes does it have, not counting the root?
cards/4/explain: The t branch: t, then e and o; under e — a and n. That is 5 nodes for three words: “t” and “te” are shared. The i branch: i, n, n — 3 more. 8 in total against 11 letters in all the words: common prefixes are stored once.
cards/4/wrong/1: 11 is the total length of the words. That many nodes would exist without shared prefixes, and here “t” and “te” are shared.
cards/4/wrong/2: 4 is the number of words. But a node is a prefix, not a word: every letter on a path has its own node.
cards/4/wrong/3: Don't forget the “inn” branch: i and two n — three nodes, shared with nothing.
cards/5/explain: The letter index is ch - 'a', from 0 to 25; ch itself is a code of 97 and up, outside the array. end goes on the last node of the path, not on the root. StartsWith is satisfied by the path existing and does not check end — otherwise it is Search. On a missing edge Find returns null: returning root would mean “found the empty prefix”.
cards/6/task: Walk the trace: card and care share the prefix car. Under the tree are next[26] and end of the current node. The rig will ask twice what the code does.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: true: all three letters were found
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: false: the path exists, but node r has end = false
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: search("car"): c, a, r — every edge is there. What does Search return?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The path “car” exists — card and care lie along it — but end on node r is set only by inserting “car” itself. Until then it is just a prefix: Search is false. StartsWith("car") on the same node answers true.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: None: it walks the edges and sets end
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: insert("car"). How many new nodes does the code create?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: All three edges c → a → r already exist: inserting card created them. Insert walks along them (??= creates nothing) and only sets end = true on node r. The prefix is stored once, and the flag tells a word from a prefix.
cards/7/q: After Insert("apple"), the call Search("app") returned true. Tap the buggy line.
cards/7/explain: end is set inside the loop — on every node of the path. After Insert("apple"), a, ap, app and appl all became “words”. Only the last node should get the flag: node.end = true belongs after the loop.
cards/8/title: next[26], a child dictionary, or nodes in an array
cards/8/body:
An array next[26] gives an O(1) step with no hashing, but costs 26 references per node however many children it has: the array is a 24-byte header plus 26 · 8 = 208 bytes, plus the node itself — about 260 bytes on 64-bit .NET. Deep in a trie a node usually has a single child, and 25 slots sit empty. And the alphabet is hard-wired: a character outside a–z gives an index outside the array.

Dictionary<char, Node> uses memory per child and accepts any alphabet: digits, _, a dot, uppercase, Cyrillic. The price is a hash on every letter and separate objects for every dictionary. For nodes with 1–3 children a small array of (letter, node) pairs with a linear scan is often cheaper.

Nodes in an array. A trie with no objects: an int[] next of size maxNodes · 26, where the child of node v by letter c is next[v * 26 + c]; 0 means “no edge” — the root is node 0, and no edge can lead to it. That is 104 bytes per node instead of ~260, not a single object for the GC, and an int array moves to a NativeArray<int> and can be walked in Burst. The size is the total word length + 1 if the dictionary is known up front; otherwise grow the array by doubling.
cards/8/deep:
Deletion and counters. To delete words and answer “how many words have this prefix” (Implement Trie II, #1804), a node keeps two counters: how many words pass through it and how many end in it. Insert increments them along the path, Erase decrements them; a node with zero words passing through can be cut off.

Compression. Long chains of single-child nodes collapse into one edge labelled with a string — a radix tree (Patricia): there are as many nodes as branchings, not letters. For a dictionary that never changes, identical endings are merged as well — the result is a minimal automaton (DAWG), several times more compact than a trie.

Characters. A char in C# is a UTF-16 code unit, not a letter: an emoji is two chars, and “é” may be one character or “e” followed by a separate accent mark. For user text, normalize the string first (Normalize()) and bring it to one case (ToLowerInvariant()).

Burst. The end flag can live in the same NativeArray<int> — a 27th slot per node — and then the whole trie is one block of memory that several jobs can safely read at once.
cards/9/q: Unity: autocomplete in the developer console. The commands are spawn_enemy, r.shadows, god2, Time.scale, a couple of hundred in total. A trie on next[26] indexed by ch - 'a' crashes on insert. What do you do?
cards/9/options/0: Keep the children in a Dictionary<char, Node>: any alphabet, and with a couple of hundred commands memory does not matter
cards/9/options/1: Keep next[26] and skip characters outside a–z on insert
cards/9/options/2: Lowercase the commands — that is enough
cards/9/options/3: Catch the IndexOutOfRangeException and skip those commands
cards/9/explain: '_' - 'a' = −2, and '.' and digits are outside the array too. A child dictionary accepts any characters and spends memory per child. There are few commands, so the cost of a hash per letter is invisible. For pure ASCII a next[128] indexed by ch would also work.
cards/9/wrong/1: Then spawn_enemy and spawnenemy become one path, and r.shadows turns into the word rshadows: autocomplete starts lying.
cards/9/wrong/2: Lowercasing removes capitals, but '_', '.' and digits stay outside a–z.
cards/9/wrong/3: The commands disappear from suggestions, and an exception on insert is a sign that the representation does not fit the data.
cards/10/title: Unity: autocomplete, a word game, a trie over bits
cards/10/body:
Autocomplete. Walk down to the prefix node, then collect the words below it with a depth-first walk until you have k suggestions. Children are visited in letter order, so the suggestions come out alphabetically. The cost is O(L + the part visited), not the whole dictionary. Need “the most frequent”? Store a ready top-k in each node.

A word game. A grid of letters, find every dictionary word in it (Word Search II, #212, hard). The depth-first walk over cells moves in step with the trie: a step to a neighbouring cell is a step along an edge. No edge — this branch cannot produce a single word, and the walk stops right there. Without a trie every word would have to be searched in the grid separately.

A trie over bits. The alphabet can have two “letters” — the bits of a number. The bit manipulation unit solves Maximum XOR of Two Numbers (#421) this way: numbers go into a trie bit by bit from the highest to the lowest, and for each number you walk down greedily — along the opposite bit whenever that edge exists.
cards/11/q: You are solving Implement Trie out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: only a–z or not, word lengths, number of calls, whether deletion is needed
cards/11/items/1: Name the naive solution: a HashSet<string>, StartsWith by scanning — O(n · L) per query
cards/11/items/2: The idea: a node is a prefix, children in next[26], an end flag at the end of a word
cards/11/items/3: Write Insert and a shared Find, then Search and StartsWith on top of it
cards/11/items/4: Walk an example: apple, then Search("app") — false, StartsWith("app") — true
cards/11/items/5: Complexity: O(L) per operation, memory O(nodes · 26)
cards/11/items/6: Bring up memory: a child dictionary or nodes in an array if the alphabet is large or there are many words
cards/11/explain: The alphabet is the first question: it decides between a child array and a dictionary. The apple and app example checks the main subtlety — the end flag. Raise memory yourself: in a Unity or .NET interview you will almost certainly be asked about 26 references per node.
cards/12/q: Match each task or question with its answer.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: The path exists and end == true
cards/12/pairs/1/1: The path exists, end does not matter
cards/12/pairs/3/1: Nodes in an int[] by number
cards/12/pairs/4/1: A trie over bits from the highest
